script.title: Your consumer rights in 2027: 5 that work when money goes wrong
script.hook: 5 rights protect your money when a company or a scammer gets it wrong, and most people never use one. Here's each one, with the deadline that matters.

segments.heading: Why this week
segments.narration: It's National Consumer Protection Week, which the Federal Trade Commission calls a time to talk about frauds, scams and consumer rights. We spend most of the year on the scams. Today is the rights: five of them, each with a deadline, each from the FTC's own pages. None of them cost anything to use. All of them work better if you know about them before you need them, so this is one to save. And if you only remember one thing, remember the deadlines, because most of these rights quietly run out if you wait.
segments.on_screen_text: NCPW: frauds, scams and your rights
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Right 1: cancel a door sale
segments.narration: Right one. Someone sells you something at your front door, or at a pop-up event in a hotel room or a fairground. Under the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule you can cancel for a full refund until midnight of the third business day after the sale. Saturdays count as business days, Sundays and federal holidays don't. It covers sales of twenty-five dollars or more at your home, and a hundred and thirty or more at temporary locations. The seller has to tell you about the right and give you two cancellation forms. Mail one back, postmarked in time, and keep a copy. The refund is due within ten days. Some sales, like real estate and insurance, aren't covered, and the FTC's page lists the exceptions.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Right 2: dispute a card charge
segments.narration: Right two. A wrong charge on your credit card: something you cancelled, never got, or never bought. Write to the card company at the billing disputes address, which isn't the address you send payments to. Your letter has to arrive within sixty days after the first bill with the error. The company must acknowledge it within thirty days and resolve it within ninety, and while it does, you can hold off paying the disputed amount. Call first if you like, but the letter is what protects you.
segments.on_screen_text: 60 days. In writing. Billing disputes address
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Maya's free trial
segments.narration: Here's how two of these rights work together, in a made-up case. Maya sees an ad for a skin cream: free, just pay four ninety-five shipping. She orders. Three weeks later her card shows eighty-nine ninety-five, and the next month another eighty-nine ninety-five. The tiny print said 'monthly deliveries', in a box that was already ticked.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a woman at a laptop looking at a card statement with two identical charges circled. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What she does
segments.narration: Maya cancels through the company's own page and screenshots the confirmation. The next month there's a third charge anyway. So she calls the number on the back of her card and disputes it, then sends a short letter to the billing disputes address, not the payment address: her name, account number, the dates, the amounts, and a copy of the cancellation screenshot. She keeps a copy of everything.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a hand sealing an envelope next to a printed screenshot and a card statement. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How it ends
segments.narration: Her letter arrives well inside sixty days of the first bill with the error. The card company acknowledges it within a month, and she doesn't have to pay the disputed amount while they look into it. The charges come off. Total cost: one evening and a stamp. And when an ad offers to 'fix her credit' for a fee afterwards, she already knows the answer.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: the same woman smiling at a phone notification showing a credit, a stamp and envelope on the desk. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Right 3: free credit reports
segments.narration: Right three. You can see your credit report from each of the three big bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, free, once a week, at AnnualCreditReport dot com. That's the only site authorized to give them out. Lookalike sites with 'free report' in the name may try to sell you something or collect your details, so type the address yourself. Look for accounts you didn't open and addresses you've never lived at. Because it's weekly now, there's no reason to wait for a bad month: pick a day each season and check.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Right 4: fix errors yourself
segments.narration: Right four. Found a mistake? Disputing it with the credit bureau, and with the business that reported it, is free. The FTC has sample letters. And here's the scam this right protects you from: it's illegal for a credit repair company to charge you before it helps you, and nobody can legally remove true, accurate information. A company that wants money up front, promises to erase real late payments, or tells you not to contact the bureaus is showing you all three red flags at once.
segments.on_screen_text: Disputes are free. Up-front fees are illegal
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Right 5: make a collector prove it
segments.narration: Right five. A debt collector has to tell you who they are, their mailing address, the creditor, and how much you owe, within five days of first contacting you. If you don't recognize the debt, dispute it within thirty days of getting that information, and they have to stop collecting until they verify it. A caller who threatens arrest and won't give you an address isn't using a right. That's the FTC's description of a fake collector.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Put them to work
segments.narration: So here's the short version to keep. Three business days for a door sale. Sixty days for a card error. Weekly credit reports, free. Fix errors yourself, free. Five days for a collector to tell you what you owe. And when a company or a scammer ignores any of this, report it at ReportFraud dot FTC dot gov. Reports are how the FTC spots patterns and builds cases. Examples in this video were fictional. Save this, and send it to whoever handles the bills in your house.
